title: Girl, 14, planned random killing of child at her former Winnipeg elementary school: Crown
summary: A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the…

image.caption: A Winnipeg teen who allegedly plotted to kill a kindergarten-aged child at random was granted bail by a judge Thursday. (Martin Diotte/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.
Teen radicalized online by 'nihilistic, violent extremism culture,' expert testifies
WARNING: This story contains references to extreme violence involving children, and teen suicide.

A 14-year-old girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.

The girl, who cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, was granted bail by provincial court Judge Lindy Choy in a Winnipeg courtroom Thursday, according to recordings reviewed by CBC News. The teen is charged with one count of uttering threats.

She was admitted to a psychiatric unit for children and youth twice since July, with the most recent instance coming after her parents found written plans to kill a kindergarten-aged child at her former elementary school in early September, Crown prosecutor Jennifer Comack said.
The girl later expressed disbelief at her release from that facility, writing she had "fool[ed] everybody," Comack said.
"I have no idea how I got away with this with no legal consequences," the girl wrote in a journal seized by police on Oct. 15, according to the prosecutor.
"I told them it was just a joke and a hypothetical and they just ... believed it??? I mean, good for me."

Comack said the girl first gained police attention in July, when she was 13, after she tried to board a flight from Winnipeg to Toronto using credit card information she secretly obtained from her parents.

She planned to take a bus to Niagara Falls and walk across the Canada-U.S. border, where an 18-year-old man would have picked her up, Comack said. The girl later told her parents she was heading there to "participate in a suicide pact," Comack said.

blocks.text: The teen was initially admitted to the psychiatric unit after the July incident, but there was a "deep escalation" and "key shift" in her behaviour upon her release, as she began to engage with "nihilistic, violent extremism culture," Comack said.

Const. Andrea Lefort, a terrorism and extremism specialist with the Winnipeg Police Service, testified on Nov. 16 that the girl was radicalized online and is a "classic" example of young people who engage with "some of the most horrific" online content involving extreme violence and gore.

Lefort said the girl engaged with online communities that seek to emulate and "almost" fantasize about previous school attackers and mass killers, particularly Dylan Klebold — one of two teen gunmen who massacred 12 students and a teacher before killing themselves at Columbine High School in Colorado in 1999.
"We do see that with this online community, where in some cases, they will not just emulate them and want to mimic them, hence them planning their attacks," the constable said.

"But, in some cases, we will see a fantasy romance. And we do see that as well with [her], where we see her talking about her love for Dylan, and even talking about maybe seeing him at some point in the future, even though he's long since deceased."
The case represents "uncharted waters" for the Winnipeg Police Service, Lefort said.
'We are scared,' mother tells judge

The girl wrote about going to her former elementary school under the guise of visiting old teachers, hiding in the washroom and killing any child who entered, then "parad[ing] the corpse around the school to terrorize the children, before fleeing and killing herself," Comack said.
"What's the fun in killing yourself if you don't take anyone down with you?" the girl wrote, according to Comack.
She also wrote about the challenge in deciding what weapon to use, the prosecutor said.

"If I was in the [United] States, this would be an easy choice — a gun, duh — but I'm in Canada, which makes this a lot harder," she wrote. "I could use a hammer since the target would be a small child, maybe a knife. I think I'll bring both."

blocks.text: In another entry, the girl said she set the attack for Nov. 2, calling it "doom hour."
"Yay!!! It's nice having an official date."

Police and the former school were alerted about the planned attack in early October, court heard. The girl was arrested as she was discharged from the psychiatric facility on Oct. 15, which is when she gave a statement to police.
The girl told police she'd had unrestricted Internet access since age seven, and watched "cartel Mexican death videos as early as that age," Comack said.
"It is chilling to watch her, in her police statement, talk so matter of fact about killing a child," the prosecutor said.

As Lefort spoke about some extreme online communities' glorification of mass killers and their lack of empathy for the victims, someone on a court recording is heard saying, "So, just for the record, she is smiling right now."
The judge later asked the teen why she was smiling.
"It's awkward," the girl replied. "It's not smiling about the case or situation, it's more so just awkward."
The girl said she wanted to "get better," as she'd recently experienced "some really insane episodes," she said.

items: Violent extremism targeting kids online an 'escalating threat': Winnipeg police

blocks.text: "Sometimes, I just get really angry about something ... stupid."
The girl's mother, who was in the courtroom alongside her father, said they love and support their daughter but, "we are scared."
Comack said the Crown didn't oppose the girl's release but wanted to ensure she'll have no access to the Internet unless supervised by someone pre-approved.

The girl agreed to that condition, as well as staying away from her former elementary school, which CBC News is not naming to protect the girl's identity as required by the Youth Criminal Justice Act.
